By confining the agent to specific folders and requiring explicit connectors, they are attempting to strike a balance between the utility of an OS-level agent and the security of a sandboxed application. What distinguishes Anthropic's approach is its bottom-up evolution. Rather than designing an AI assistant and retrofitting agent capabilities, Anthropic built a powerful coding agent first — Claude Code — and is now abstracting its capabilities for broader audiences. This technical lineage may give Cowork more robust agentic behavior from the start. Claude Code has generated significant enthusiasm among developers since its initial launch as a command-line tool in late 2024. The company expanded access with a web interface in October 2025, followed by a Slack integration in December. Cowork is the next logical step: bringing the same agentic architecture to users who may never touch a terminal. For now, Cowork remains exclusive to Claude Max subscribers using the macOS desktop application. Users on other subscription tiers — Free, Pro, Team, or Enterprise — can join a waitlist for future access. Anthropic has signaled clear intentions to expand the feature's reach. The blog post explicitly mentions plans to add cross-device sync and bring Cowork to Windows as the company learns from the research preview. Cherny set expectations appropriately, describing the product as "early and raw, similar to what Claude Code felt like when it first launched." To access Cowork, Max subscribers can download or update the Claude macOS app and click on "Cowork" in the sidebar. For technical decision-makers, the implications of Cowork extend beyond any single product launch. The bottleneck for AI adoption is shifting — no longer is model intelligence the limiting factor, but rather workflow integration and user trust. Anthropic's goal, as the company puts it, is to make working with Claude feel less like operating a tool and more like delegating to a colleague. Whether mainstream users are ready to hand over folder access to an AI that might misinterpret their instructions remains an open question. But the speed of Cowork's development — a major feature built in ten days, possibly by the company's own AI — previews a future where the capabilities of these systems compound faster than organizations can evaluate them. The chatbot has learned to use a file manager. What it learns to use next is anyone's guess.

articles.headline: Apple's Foldable iPhone Will Help Bring Some Magic Back
articles.blurb: Apple is set to introduce its foldable iPhone at a launch event on or around September 9. Samsung has stolen some of the thunder from the launch by introducing a similar design, but that just reinforces that the new form factor is a winner. Apple's device reportedly excels as a camera viewfinder, but it lacks a telephoto camera, which could be an issue for early adopters spending over $2,000. The design also relies on Touch ID rather than Face ID.

articles.headline: Nvidia Customers Notified About AI-Related Price Hikes Above 15%
articles.blurb: Some of Nvidia's biggest customers have been told that the price of the AI servers containing its flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips is going up by more than 15% due to the soaring costs of memory chips. The price hikes will go into effect early next year. The increases will depend on the generation of Nvidia chips and the memory configurations. Nvidia has also raised prices for its gaming-oriented PC graphics cards.

articles.headline: Amazon's Toaster-Shaped Robotaxis Are Hitting the Road
articles.blurb: Amazon's all-electric toaster-shaped Zoox taxis are the first robotaxis offering rides on the roads without standard driver features like a dashboard or pedals. They can drive in either direction and hold up to four passengers sitting facing each other. Amazon has started rolling out the vehicles across San Francisco and Las Vegas. Tesla's Cybercab lacks a steering wheel and pedals, but it has not received the same regulatory approval as Zoox to begin offering rides to the public.

articles.headline: Chinese humanoid robots smash human records in 100m sprint and high jump at Beijing robot games
articles.blurb: The opening day of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday saw Chinese humanoid robots break records set by humans, including Usain Bolt's 100-meter sprint world record. More than 2,000 humanoid robots participated in the event. There were 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions, including running, table tennis, and soccer. While the games showcased humanoid robots' rapidly evolving abilities, experts say it will still take time to achieve mass real-world deployment and that these robots are mostly still used for demonstrations, performances, and research.

articles.headline: There's no reason for software to be slow anymore
articles.blurb: A lot of the tedium it used to take to get a tricky optimization working is now gone. Many optimizations that were previously too risky to try make sense to try out now. AI drastically reduces the cost of optimization. It can turn days or weeks of work into a trivial loop.

articles.headline: The New MCP Roadmap
articles.blurb: The updated roadmap for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) sets the direction for protocol work over the coming months. It is organized into five priority areas: agentic messaging primitives, HTTP-native transport unification and hardening, agent identity and enterprise-ready security, improved primitives, and improved SDK developer experience. Specification Enhancement Proposals that fall within these priority areas get expedited review and have the best chance of acceptance.

articles.headline: ‘Maybe I'm Psycho': Why Tech Founders And VCs Are So Online
articles.blurb: New news is coming out so fast that it seems crazy for a founder not to be fully plugged in. Being online can help build a presence and keep people as informed as possible. Posting frequently can help drive inbound interest. Tech Twitter can provide a view of emerging consensus, but few immediately actionable insights. It's important to actively maintain cognitive security and cognitive hygiene, as spending too much time online can be dangerous.

articles.headline: Fable & The End of the Free Lunch
articles.blurb: When Moore's Law was in full effect, it didn't make sense to ruthlessly optimize code, as a new CPU would arrive in 18 months that would double performance. Developers only started to have to think about parallelization, architecture, memory locality, etc, after Moore's Law started slowing down in the mid-2000s. Prior to Fable, it felt like a waste to spend too much time improving coding harnesses or context strategies, as a new model would arrive at the same price or cheaper in just a few months that would cover most of the problem. Fable is incredible, but the cost is so high that developers are now starting to think about what work should go where and optimizing their harnesses to provide weaker models with sufficient context to perform well.

articles.headline: An agent.md to improve LLM-assisted code quality
articles.blurb: A good coding harness can help improve code quality dramatically.

articles.headline: The asteroid currently hitting frontend web development
articles.blurb: The front end is less risky to just hand to an agent, so many AI coders will feel comfortable just letting their agents handle it unsupervised.

articles.headline: How I Find Problems to Solve as a Staff Engineer
articles.blurb: Finding problems comes from staying engaged with people's work long enough to see what no single request can show you.

articles.headline: Nvidia Is Spending $6 Billion to Build a Powerful US Alternative to Chinese AI
articles.blurb: Nvidia will invest $1 billion in AI startup Poolside at a pre-money valuation of $12 billion and will pay $6 billion to license Poolside's technology and hire the bulk of its engineers.

articles.headline: Fast and Hard Code
articles.blurb: AI enables developers to pick less common languages and work with much harder technologies.

articles.headline: Starting a quantitative trading firm with 0 experience
articles.blurb: Table/game selection is just as important as execution, especially in markets.

articles.headline: Startup Founders Are Working Harder Than Ever to Keep Up With Their AI Agents
articles.blurb: Founders have long put in long hours in the name of building the next big thing, but AI agents are pushing this to the next level. AI agents' growing capabilities and the speed at which the models powering them are evolving are causing founders to work more and more as they fear missing out on precious hours of work. This is causing erratic sleep schedules, a struggle to focus on anything but work, and the feeling that, while the pace is unhealthy and unsustainable, they just can't stop.

articles.headline: Will the DOJ's investigation into a16z spook other VCs?
articles.blurb: The DOJ has spent close to a year on an antitrust probe of Andreessen Horowitz, and the subject is board seats like the ones your own investors hold. Regulators are looking at partners sitting on boards of AI companies that now compete, with Ben Horowitz at Databricks and Martin Casado at Fivetran named as examples. If firms respond by giving up seats or declining them, board composition, information rights, and term sheets change for anyone raising now. Nobody outside the probe knows what the underlying allegations are.

articles.headline: Build vs Buy When Building Just Got Cheap
articles.blurb: For most of the last two decades, building a custom alternative was rarely worth it. That's now changed - building something fitted specifically to your company is now cheap. However, what hasn't changed is risk, security, and total cost of ownership. The reasons to not build auth in-house are still the same as they always were.

articles.headline: Building a semantic layer: What it is and how we did it at PostHog
articles.blurb: A semantic layer is a dictionary of definitions that agents and humans read from. It doesn't copy data, replace a warehouse, or move a single row of data. It sits on top of the data that exists and describes it. The semantic layer gives everyone a single place to read definitions from so that the team is on the same page. This post tells the story of how PostHog built a semantic layer into its context warehouse.

articles.headline: Skills for your whole team are here
articles.blurb: Notion skills teach agents how teams work so they don't have to start from scratch. Users can ask Notion Agents to turn teams' work into skills that can be shared. Skills are Notion pages. Users can add processes, examples, references, and preferred formats, then share them like any other page.

articles.headline: The X Ads MCP
articles.blurb: The X Ads MCP allows users to create ads directly from where they already use agents. Users can connect Grok, Grok Build, Claude Code, or other AI agents directly to their X Ads accounts and manage campaigns through normal conversation. Agents can pull real campaign data, analyze the results, and tell users what's working and what's not. The AI can create and manage campaigns, search interests and locations for targeting, add or remove targeting, create ad posts, promote existing posts, check campaign performance and reach, and update and activate campaigns. There are 23 X Ads tools available through the MCP.

articles.headline: Why your local LLM feels dumber than it is
articles.blurb: Plenty of teams save money running open AI models on their own hardware, shrunk to fit. Someone on a forum tested those shrunken versions of one model and logged 44.8 terabytes of results. Same model, same question. Right answer on one graphics card, wrong answer split across two, right again across four. One common compression setting quietly broke the model's ability to call outside tools, while a slightly bigger one worked fine. A feature that flakes in production but sails through your demo may be a settings problem, not a code problem. Answers also drift deep into long documents.

articles.headline: How the GTM playbook has changed in 2026
articles.blurb: Inbound came out as the most-adopted go-to-market motion in this benchmark survey of B2B software companies, at 23%. Product-led growth still dominates below $1M ARR and under $5K ACV, so where your company sits decides which numbers apply. Channel use runs LinkedIn 66%, SEO 53%, warm outbound 48%. Some 47% of teams are testing AI discovery channels, and answer-engine optimization is the top rising investment. Hybrid pricing sits at 37%, and AI credit models are forecast to grow 114% in twelve months. On hiring, 39% of top AI companies are filling forward-deployed roles at $213K to $370K+.

articles.blurb: Companies often overlook the customer experience with third-party services that carry their branding, leading to inefficiencies and frustration.

articles.headline: Say it once: introducing Bot Preference Sync
articles.blurb: Cloudflare now writes AI bot policies into robots.txt automatically across Search, Agent, and Training categories on every plan for free.

articles.headline: Docker Verified Publisher Apps Are Now Self-Serve
articles.blurb: Docker has made its Verified Publisher program self-serve, so software vendors can now apply directly through Docker Hub instead of going through a sales team. Approved publishers get a verified badge, prioritized search ranking, and access to analytics that identify which companies are pulling their images. The badge covers all content types on Docker Hub, including MCP servers, models, sandboxes, and agents. Current verified publishers include Google, Microsoft, AWS, Datadog, and Grafana Labs.

articles.headline: AWS Glue 6.0 now available with 30% lower price and full Apache Iceberg v3 support
articles.blurb: AWS Glue 6.0 is now generally available in all AWS regions where Glue operates, with pricing 30% lower than previous versions. The release is built on Apache Spark 4.1, Python 3.13, and Scala 2.13, and includes full support for the Apache Iceberg v3 specification via Iceberg 1.11.0. A new VARIANT data type with shredding support lets teams store and query JSON, logs, and event data without flattening schemas. No API changes are required to use the new version.

articles.headline: DigitalOcean Inference Router, Now Cache-Aware: Why the Cheapest Model Isn't Always the Best Deal
articles.blurb: DigitalOcean has added cache-aware routing to its Inference Router, letting the system account for the cost of breaking a warm prompt cache when deciding whether to switch models mid-session. The update pairs with two new controls: an explicit model affinity header that ties requests to a session, and a routing budget parameter that caps how much extra cost a model switch can incur.

articles.headline: Quick thoughts on Azure Regional Outage from July 23, '26
articles.blurb: A July 23 Azure West US outage lasted about five hours after a networking repair triggered an unexpectedly broad device isolation. Contributing factors included flawed blast radius analysis, inadequate aggregate safety validation, misleading health signals, incomplete event logging, and rollback automation that depended on the disrupted connectivity.

articles.headline: Octopus Easy Mode - Kubernetes Microservice Orchestration
articles.blurb: Octopus can orchestrate independently deployable Kubernetes microservices through a parent project using Deploy a Release steps, coordinating sequential or parallel deployments across environments. The approach preserves individual service deployment while enabling teams to promote multiple services together as a single unit with consistent lifecycle management.

articles.headline: Databasus (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Databasus is a free, open source, self-hosted backup tool for PostgreSQL that supports storage backends like S3, Google Drive, and FTP, plus notifications via Slack, Discord, and Telegram. It focuses on Point-in-Time Recovery and verifies backups by performing actual restores, not just checking files on disk.

articles.headline: Aerospork (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: AeroSpork is a fork of AeroSpace, an i3-style tiling window manager for macOS. It adds a settings GUI, notarized universal builds for both arm64 and x86_64, and a fix for monitor identity that uses CoreGraphics UUIDs instead of IOKit.

articles.headline: How CISA's BOD 26-04 changes vulnerability prioritization
articles.blurb: CISA's Binding Operational Directive 26-04 requires federal agencies to prioritize vulnerability remediation by actual risk rather than static severity scores. This post describes how Datadog's tools help teams identify and remediate the critical findings the directive targets.

articles.headline: Wild AI-Related Reliability Incidents Are Coming
articles.blurb: AI agents acting as autonomous first responders may successfully resolve many routine incidents, but their ability to take operational actions also creates new failure modes when they encounter situations they cannot handle. The most dangerous scenario is an agent attempting remediation in an unexpected way, making an already complex outage worse before humans enter the loop and forcing responders to diagnose the combined behavior of the software system and the agent itself.

articles.headline: There Continue to Be Reasons for Software to Be Slow
articles.blurb: LLMs can make performance work cheaper to implement, but implementation cost is often not the main reason optimizations do not ship: teams may tolerate slower software, cut engineering budgets, deprioritize performance, or face larger costs in testing, migration, correctness, and long-term maintenance. AI-generated optimizations can also overfit benchmarks or introduce reliability problems, so faster code generation does not necessarily translate into faster production software.

articles.headline: Google Agent2Agent Protocol Joins AAIF
articles.blurb: Google's Agent2Agent Protocol, an open standard for cross-vendor agent communication, is joining the Agentic AI Foundation alongside the Linux Foundation-backed MCP ecosystem.

articles.headline: Sandboxing local AI Agents
articles.blurb: Local AI coding agents run arbitrary prompts with full access to a developer's machine, risking accidental or malicious file deletion and secret exfiltration.

articles.headline: Banks looking to insure against AI hallucination
articles.blurb: Testudo, a Lloyd's-backed startup, is offering coverage of up to $10 million for liabilities arising from generative AI, with annual premiums typically ranging from $10,000 to $20,000. Interest is emerging as financial institutions consider deploying tools that can interact with customers or execute transactions, although some vendors prefer to guarantee their own products and skeptics question whether a separate category of coverage is necessary.

articles.headline: Washington goes all-in on crypto as CLARITY Act negotiations intensify
articles.blurb: President Donald Trump urged lawmakers to pass a “fair version” of the CLARITY Act as crypto executives met with the White House over remaining disputes, particularly ethics provisions tied to government officials' crypto interests. At the same time, the CFTC warned it could use existing authority to build its own crypto regulatory regime if Congress stalls, while the SEC proposed its first crypto-specific fundraising framework with new exemptions and a conditional safe harbor.

articles.headline: JPMorgan debanked Polymarket last year over regulatory concerns, source says
articles.blurb: JPMorgan ended a banking relationship with Polymarket in October 2025 as prediction markets faced growing scrutiny from regulators over their resemblance to gambling. Polymarket pushed back on the characterization of the relationship, saying it continues to work closely with the bank across multiple entities and customer fund flows. The episode highlights the regulatory uncertainty surrounding the fast-growing prediction market sector, with platforms including Polymarket and Kalshi facing increased attention from state officials.

articles.headline: Inside Max Levchin's slow-and-steady path to Affirm profitability
articles.blurb: Affirm has finally reached profitability after years of heavy investment and more than $2 billion in cumulative losses, validating Max Levchin's long-term strategy of building much of the company's technology and risk infrastructure in-house. That philosophy can be traced back to Levchin's experience fighting fraud at PayPal. The same operational discipline helped turn Affirm into a roughly $25 billion fintech company.

articles.headline: System of Action Part 4: The case for the application layer
articles.blurb: Foundation models alone cannot reliably “do the work” inside most businesses because real jobs require domain-specific workflows, deterministic software, permissions, semantics, human escalation, and continuous learning loops. There is a major opportunity for vertical SaaS incumbents and AI-native challengers to become the System of Action for their industries, potentially expanding software TAM by roughly 10x by capturing labor spend rather than just software budgets.

articles.headline: Airwallex expands from cross-border payments into autonomous finance
articles.blurb: Airwallex is using its recent $320 million Series H at an $11 billion valuation to expand beyond cross-border payments into autonomous finance, including T:0 for automated bookkeeping and Airi for agentic commerce. The company now serves more than 675,000 businesses with over $1 billion in annualized revenue, but president Lucy Liu says an IPO still depends on market conditions as Airwallex expands globally and navigates growing regulatory scrutiny in the US and Australia.

articles.headline: PayPal and Venmo expand into college tuition payments
articles.blurb: PayPal and Venmo have integrated with Illumia, Nelnet Campus Commerce, and TouchNet to let students and parents pay tuition directly through participating college payment portals. The move expands PayPal's campus strategy beyond peer-to-peer payments and athletics, giving Venmo and PayPal access to thousands of higher-education institutions through existing payments infrastructure.

articles.headline: Citadel unwinds more than 80% of risk from Situational Awareness portfolio
articles.blurb: Ken Griffin said Citadel has shed more than 80% of the risk from the portfolio it acquired from Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness, using more than 100 block trades representing over $4 billion in market value. The deal came after the AI-focused hedge fund was forced to liquidate public positions amid steep losses, while Citadel's flagship Wellington fund returned 5.94% in July, its best month since 2022.

articles.headline: JPMorgan hires Bank of America's David Fishman to lead North America technology M&A
articles.blurb: JPMorgan is hiring veteran Bank of America dealmaker David Fishman as head of North America technology M&A, while elevating Vineet Seth to vice chair of investment banking and forming a new advisory group for key technology clients. The move adds to a broader talent reshuffling across Wall Street tech banking, with several senior Bank of America executives recently departing for JPMorgan, Barclays, Deutsche Bank, and Citi.

articles.headline: Ripple raises $275M in bond financing to grow US business
articles.blurb: Ripple Prime plans to use the new capital to expand its multi-asset clearing, financing, and prime brokerage services in the US.

articles.headline: Francisco Partners acquires Weave for $650M
articles.blurb: Francisco Partners agreed to acquire healthcare payments and communications software provider Weave for $650 million, taking the company private and backing further investment in AI.

articles.headline: AI data centers could be first to lose power when the grid is strained
articles.blurb: PJM is proposing rules that would make some new large-load customers, including AI data centers, interruptible when electricity supply gets tight. The proposal highlights how power availability is becoming a limiting factor for AI infrastructure growth.

articles.headline: Alibaba launches $10B share sale to fund AI expansion
articles.blurb: Alibaba plans to raise roughly $10 billion to expand its AI infrastructure, chips, data centers, and model development. The raise comes days after the company reported a 75% jump in capex tied largely to AI.

articles.headline: Sam Altman on building OpenAI and betting on the impossible (78 minute podcast)
articles.blurb: Sam Altman discusses OpenAI's early non-consensus bets, scaling compute, AI adoption, and why society may absorb AI more slowly than model progress suggests. He also argues AI could enable a boom in small businesses while warning against concentrating control of the technology among too few players.

articles.headline: The AI-Native SDLC playbook
articles.blurb: Anthropic lays out how AI changes software development beyond simply adding coding assistants, including planning, implementation, review, and operations. It argues teams need to redesign development workflows around agents rather than bolt them onto existing processes.

articles.headline: Nvidia backs Cloverleaf to expand AI data center infrastructure
articles.blurb: Nvidia made a minority investment in Cloverleaf Infrastructure. The companies have partnered to develop AI factories across the US. Cloverleaf says its pipeline already includes multiple gigawatt-scale infrastructure projects.

articles.headline: Ramp launches an AI model router
articles.blurb: Ramp has opened the internal model-routing infrastructure it uses across more than 100 AI use cases as a standalone product. Router can automatically choose models based on cost, quality, latency, and availability. Ramp says it cut its own LLM costs by roughly 30%.

articles.headline: GitLab 19.3 helps enterprises scale agentic development securely
articles.blurb: The GitLab 19.3 update is aimed at helping enterprises scale agentic software development while retaining control over data, permissions, and spending. The release adds single-tenant deployment for the Duo Agent Platform, Secrets Manager support beyond pipelines, bulk SAST remediation, plain-language custom flow creation, and usage caps for agentic AI.

articles.headline: AI agents are turning enterprise data silos into an infrastructure problem
articles.blurb: Enterprise data stacks were largely designed around human access patterns, but agents need reliable real-time access across systems. That is turning data integration and context infrastructure into a prerequisite for successful agent deployments.

articles.headline: The GPU bill is becoming the new AWS bill
articles.blurb: Enterprises risk repeating the cloud cost-management mistakes of the last decade as expensive GPU infrastructure proliferates. AI teams increasingly need FinOps-style controls for utilization, capacity planning, and workload economics.

articles.headline: Anthropic plans customer-controlled storage for frontier-model data
articles.blurb: Anthropic plans to let enterprises keep required retained data inside their own cloud infrastructure rather than Anthropic's systems.

articles.headline: Portworx Enterprise 3.6.2.2 adds stronger vSphere certificate verification
articles.blurb: The release adds TLS certificate verification for vCenter connections during cloud-drive operations and includes several Kubernetes and disaster-recovery fixes.

articles.headline: Who’s Tracking You? Use This New Service to Find Out
articles.blurb: It can be daunting to determine who's responsible for showing ads on the websites we visit, or who's harvesting data from the mobile apps we use every day. That information is already semi-public, but it is not easily parsed and traditionally much of it has remained walled away in the hands of large advertising platforms. Not anymore: A powerful and free new service called DecryptAds scrapes and correlates this adtech data and makes it simple to quickly learn a great deal about the entities that are tracking you.

articles.headline: Microsoft Plugs Nearly 400 Security Holes
articles.blurb: Microsoft today released updates to remedy at least 398 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software, including one weakness that is already being actively exploited and two others that were publicly detailed prior to today.

articles.headline: Canadian Man Pleads Guilty in Snowflake Extortions
articles.blurb: A 26-year-old Canadian man once described as one of the most consequential cybercrime threat actors of 2024 has pleaded guilty to computer fraud and conspiracy to hack and extort more than 165 organizations that used the cloud data storage provider Snowflake. Connor Riley Moucka, of Kitchener, Ontario, also admitted to stealing call and text history records of more than 100 million AT&T customers.

articles.headline: Read This Before You Buy That TV Streaming Stick
articles.blurb: Security experts have been sounding the alarm for years about the risks of using generic TV boxes that promise unlimited content streaming for a one-time fee, warning that they secretly rent the user's Internet connection out to strangers. But a groundbreaking new analysis finds these devices also routinely spoof themselves as mobile phones clicking ads on AI-generated websites as part of sprawling operation that seeks to defraud online merchants and advertising networks.

articles.headline: LG to Ban Residential Proxies from Smart TV Apps
articles.blurb: The home appliance giant LG Electronics USA said this week it plans to suspend any apps built for its smart TVs that turn one's television into an always-on residential proxy node. The move comes less than a month after researchers found that more than 42 percent of games and other apps available for download on LG's webOS store allow unknown third-parties to route their Internet traffic through a user's TV.

articles.headline: Microsoft Patches a Record 570 Security Flaws
articles.blurb: Microsoft Corp. today released software updates to plug at least 570 security holes in its Windows operating systems and other software, almost triple the number of vulnerabilities the software giant fixed in its record-smashing Patch Tuesday release last month. Microsoft attributed the burgeoning patch counts to vulnerability discoveries aided by artificial intelligence.

articles.headline: Lessons Learned from CISA’s Recent GitHub Leak
articles.blurb: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued a postmortem on a data leak in which a contractor published dozens of internal CISA credentials -- including AWS Govcloud keys -- in a public GitHub repository for almost six months before being notified by KrebsOnSecurity. Experts say the gaps identified in the agency's initial response provide important lessons that all security teams should absorb.

articles.headline: Felons, Fraudsters Flog Offensive Cybersecurity Startup
articles.blurb: A cybersecurity startup dangling millions of dollars to acquire zero-day security vulnerabilities in popular software is run by a pair of far-right conspiracy theorists and convicted felons whose most recent ventures included fake intelligence companies and a now-defunct AI-based lobbying platform they operated under assumed names.

articles.headline: FBI Seizes NetNut Proxy Platform, Popa Botnet
articles.blurb: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said today it worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, a sprawling residential proxy service operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies [NASDAQ: ALAR]. The action comes roughly two weeks after KrebsOnSecurity published findings from multiple security firms connecting NetNut to the Popa botnet, a collection of at least two million devices that have been compromised by malicious software with little or no consent from victims.

articles.headline: Scattered Spider Hackers Plead Guilty on Day 1 of Trial
articles.blurb: Two men pleaded guilty in the United Kingdom this week to criminal charges stemming from an August 2024 cyberattack that crippled Transport for London, the entity responsible for the public transport network in the Greater London area. The duo were key members of a prolific cybercrime group known as Scattered Spider, and their guilty pleas came on the first day of what was expected to be a six-week trial.

articles.headline: Children make up half of mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreads
articles.blurb: West African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetected More than half of the mpox cases reported in Guinea-Bissau have been among children, local authorities have said, almost two months since the country announced an epidemic. A national outbreak was declared on 4 July, just over a week after a 27-year-old woman became the first confirmed case of mpox in the west African country. Since then, there have been seven confirmed cases and 46 suspected cases. Half of those patients have been children, with 16 under the age of four.

The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.
